problem: Rule-based frontier and information-theoretic exploration depends on hand-crafted map features and stopping rules, and does not adapt well to new environments. End-to-end DRL exploration, which maps raw sensor data to control, learns slowly and transfers poorly from simulation to a real robot because of sensor and mechanical gaps.
motivation: Autonomous exploration (building a full map of an unknown environment) underpins rescue and cleaning robots, and it tests how well a robot adapts. The authors observe that the partial occupancy grid map is a compact, sim/real-invariant state from which a learner can pick the next goal. Mature SLAM and path planners can then handle safe low-level motion, so RL only has to learn the high-level 'where to go next / when to stop' decision.
key_idea: Split exploration into mapping, decision and planning modules, and learn only the decision module: a fully convolutional dueling Q-network (with an auxiliary edge-segmentation head) reads the partial occupancy grid plus robot-position maps, scores rasterized goal points and a terminal 'stop' action, and hands the chosen goal to A*+TEB for execution.
insight: Making the learned component a map-level goal selector keeps the policy simple and allows sim-to-real transfer: in the real world AFCQN keeps 0.84 explored rate vs 0.92 in sim. The standard fully connected DQN collapses to 0.54 with std 0.4173 (Table III), showing that a flatten+FC head overfits to input statistics. Replacing the FC head with a fully convolutional one (FCQN) speeds learning, cuts parameters and allows arbitrary map sizes; standard DQN cannot even run on the differently sized test maps 3–4. Adding the obstacle-contour/frontier segmentation auxiliary task (AFCQN) gives faster convergence and higher coverage (0.91 vs 0.85 on the training map) at the cost of longer paths and lower efficiency (1226.12 vs 1634.00). The learned Q-maps concentrate on frontiers, so the network rediscovers the frontier heuristic, but it also learns when to stop and avoids the frontier method's failure mode where the robot sits on the frontier centroid.
method: Modular framework: mapping module (graph-based SLAM; the paper variously names Karto SLAM, gmapping, and scan-matching front end + g2o back end) produces the occupancy grid and pose. Decision module g_t = f(l_0:t, m_t) outputs the next goal. Planning module uses A* as global planner and timed-elastic-band (TEB) as local planner, which converts the path into velocities and avoids unmapped obstacles from live LiDAR.

Entropy-based reward: from the objective min ||m − m̂||² + path length, reward r_t = α(H(m_{t-1}) − H(m_t) − L(x_{t-1}, x_t)), using Shannon entropy of the occupancy grid. Safety penalties are −1 if the goal is in unknown space or too close to an obstacle.
Terminal action: a learned stop action is rewarded +1 if explored-region ratio ρ > 0.85, else −1; ρ balances coverage vs efficiency.
Action space: goal points rasterized-sampled from the occupancy grid (discrete), plus the terminal action.

FCQN (fully convolutional dueling Q-network): the conv encoder output has the same spatial size as the action grid. A 1×1-conv branch gives a per-point advantage score map. A global-maxpool + FC branch gives the terminal-action advantage and state value V(s). Q values follow dueling aggregation Q = V + (A − mean A); trained with DQN (experience replay, target net).

AFCQN auxiliary task: a third branch of two deconvolutions segments the input map into 3 classes (obstacle contours, frontiers, other) with pixel-wise cross-entropy. Its gradient is added to the shared encoder with weight λ.
Input state: stacked images of the built grid map, a current-position map and a last-position map; greedy action selection at test time.

setting.backbone: FCQN / AFCQN: small fully convolutional dueling Q-network (trained from scratch with DQN)
setting.training_data: RL in a single virtual training map (161×201 grid, 5×8 m) in the ROS Stage simulator, ~600 training episodes; no external data
setting.observation: 2D LiDAR (+odometry) → SLAM occupancy grid map, plus rendered current- and last-position maps
setting.action_space: discrete goal points sampled on a raster over the occupancy grid + terminal/stop action; A* global planner + TEB local planner produce velocities (omnidirectional base)
setting.privileged: none (pose and map come from onboard SLAM)

numbers_note: The paper prints explored region rate as a fraction (e.g. 0.91); it is converted to 0-100 here. Path length is in meters; exploration efficiency is entropy reduction per unit path length. Tables also give std values, omitted here. Results on the four generalization test maps (Test map 1–4; AFCQN/FCQN/DQN and AFCQN vs frontier) appear only as bar charts (Fig. 9, 11, 12), with no numeric values. The number of real-world trials is not stated. This is a custom small-scale 2D exploration setup, not a standard embodied-navigation benchmark.
results: On the training map (50 random starts), AFCQN reaches the highest explored-region rate: 0.91 vs 0.85 for FCQN and 0.84 for standard DQN. FCQN has the best efficiency (1634.00) because it stops earlier. On the physical DJI Robomaster, AFCQN achieves 0.84 explored rate and the best exploration efficiency (863.82), beating the classic frontier-based method (0.91 rate but 840.79 efficiency, longer paths). Standard DQN collapses in the real world (0.54 ± 0.4173). The frontier method retains higher coverage in both sim (0.95) and real, whereas AFCQN trades a little coverage for shorter, better-terminated exploration.
limitations: The action space is a discrete rasterized grid of goal points, so decision sequences are suboptimal. The policy has no recurrent memory; both points are acknowledged by the authors.

Evaluation is very small-scale: one 5×8 m training map, four small 2D Stage test maps and one real arena. Test-map results are given only as charts. There is no comparison to learned exploration baselines such as end-to-end DRL, only to DQN and the frontier heuristic.
The frontier-based baseline achieves higher explored-region rate in every setting. Gains come mainly in efficiency and stopping, and depend on the hand-set ρ = 0.85 threshold.
compares_to: Standard DQN (fully connected head) within the same framework
